title: How a Signal Marks One Protein

scenes.tts: A cell holds many proteins. How can oxygen make it destroy H I F 1 alpha and spare the rest? Watch the target, not the tag. Yellow ubiquitin is reusable. Grey proteins are possible targets. Green E 3 is the selector.
scenes.caption: A cell holds many proteins. How can oxygen make it destroy HIF-1α and spare the rest? Watch the target, not the tag. Yellow ubiquitin is reusable. Grey proteins are possible targets. Green E3 is the selector.
scenes.visual: COLOR MAP for both films: ubiquitin yellow, targets grey, E1 blue, E2 teal, E3 or substrate receptor green, signal gold, proteasome red. Fill the frame with a moving field of grey target blocks. A single HIF-1α block remains centered as yellow ubiquitin blocks circulate and the green E3 grip opens nearby. Show the question above the target.
scenes.narration: A cell holds many proteins. How can oxygen make it destroy HIF-1α and spare the rest? Watch the target, not the tag. Yellow ubiquitin is reusable. Grey proteins are possible targets. Green E3 is the selector.

scenes.visual: Transform the question into the title 'How a Signal Marks One Protein' for two seconds, then shrink it into the upper-left corner. Keep the same HIF-1α block and circulating ubiquitin visible.

scenes.tts: E 1 spends A T P to activate ubiquitin, then holds it temporarily. E 2 receives and carries that activated tag. E 3 brings loaded E 2 beside a target it recognizes. Ubiquitin usually lands on a target lysine. The tag is common; recognition makes the transfer selective.
scenes.caption: E1 spends ATP to activate ubiquitin, then holds it temporarily. E2 receives and carries that activated tag. E3 brings loaded E2 beside a target it recognizes. Ubiquitin usually lands on a target lysine. The tag is common; recognition makes the transfer selective.
scenes.visual: Build a left-to-right relay across most of the frame. A yellow ubiquitin block lifts with an ATP token onto blue E1, transfers to teal E2, then moves beside the centered grey target when the green E3 grip closes. Finish with ubiquitin attached to a labelled lysine on the target.
scenes.narration: E1 spends ATP to activate ubiquitin, then holds it temporarily. E2 receives and carries that activated tag. E3 brings loaded E2 beside a target it recognizes. Ubiquitin usually lands on a target lysine. The tag is common; recognition makes the transfer selective.

scenes.tts: The same relay can serve many targets because the selector can change. Different E 3 receptors fit different target features. E 1 and E 2 keep ubiquitin moving. The E 3 receptor decides which grey block enters the green grip.
scenes.caption: The same relay can serve many targets because the selector can change. Different E3 receptors fit different target features. E1 and E2 keep ubiquitin moving. The E3 receptor decides which grey block enters the green grip.
scenes.visual: Keep blue E1 and teal E2 fixed at left. Cycle three large grey target blocks past two differently shaped green grips. Each grip closes only on its matching notch, while yellow ubiquitin continues moving along the relay. Label the notches 'target feature'.
scenes.narration: The same relay can serve many targets because the selector can change. Different E3 receptors fit different target features. E1 and E2 keep ubiquitin moving. The E3 receptor decides which grey block enters the green grip.

scenes.tts: A degron is the target feature an E 3 recognizes. It can be a short sequence, a chemical change, or both. Signals can create that feature or strengthen its contact. Signals change protein fate by changing what an E 3 can recognize. Now follow oxygen into this rule.
scenes.caption: A degron is the target feature an E3 recognizes. It can be a short sequence, a chemical change, or both. Signals can create that feature or strengthen its contact. Signals change protein fate by changing what an E3 can recognize. Now follow oxygen into this rule.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the matching notch and label it 'degron'. Morph a plain notch into one carrying a small gold modification badge. As the exact guiding rule appears briefly, the green grip closes. Then transform the grey target label to HIF-1α and the green grip label to VHL.
scenes.narration: A degron is the target feature an E3 recognizes. It can be a short sequence, a chemical change, or both. Signals can create that feature or strengthen its contact. Signals change protein fate by changing what an E3 can recognize. Now follow oxygen into this rule.

scenes.tts: H I F 1 alpha is made continuously in the cells pictured here. When oxygen is available, a prolyl hydroxylase uses it as a reaction substrate. The enzyme adds a hydroxyl group to a proline on H I F 1 alpha. That small badge completes a degron.
scenes.caption: HIF-1α is made continuously in the cells pictured here. When oxygen is available, a prolyl hydroxylase uses it as a reaction substrate. The enzyme adds a hydroxyl group to a proline on HIF-1α. That small badge completes a degron.
scenes.visual: A steady conveyor introduces grey HIF-1α blocks from the left. Gold oxygen dots enter a large labelled PHD block above the conveyor. Each completed reaction places a small gold OH badge on the target's proline notch. Keep all shapes schematic and show no molecular structure.
scenes.narration: HIF-1α is made continuously in the cells pictured here. When oxygen is available, a prolyl hydroxylase uses it as a reaction substrate. The enzyme adds a hydroxyl group to a proline on HIF-1α. That small badge completes a degron.

scenes.tts: Here are two H I F 1 alpha targets. One carries the hydroxyl badge, and one does not. Which target will V H L grip?
scenes.caption: Here are two HIF-1α targets. One carries the hydroxyl badge, and one does not. Which target will VHL grip?
scenes.visual: Place two equally sized HIF-1α blocks side by side. The left has a gold OH badge; the right has a plain proline notch. Center one open green VHL grip between them and place the question above. Let the targets drift slightly but reveal no answer.
scenes.narration: Here are two HIF-1α targets. One carries the hydroxyl badge, and one does not. Which target will VHL grip?

scenes.visual: Hold the prediction question and both targets for four and a half seconds. A thin countdown arc advances without numbers while VHL remains centered and open.

scenes.tts: V H L closes around the hydroxylated target. A peptide with hydroxyproline bound V H L tightly without cell extract. The same peptide with ordinary proline did not. The modification itself supplies the recognized feature.
scenes.caption: VHL closes around the hydroxylated target. A peptide with hydroxyproline bound VHL tightly without cell extract. The same peptide with ordinary proline did not. The modification itself supplies the recognized feature.
scenes.visual: Clear the question. Move green VHL onto the badged target and close the grip; let the plain target pass untouched. Beneath them, animate a simple two-row binding assay labelled 'hydroxyproline: binds' and 'ordinary proline: no binding'. Mark the assay 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: VHL closes around the hydroxylated target. A peptide with hydroxyproline bound VHL tightly without cell extract. The same peptide with ordinary proline did not. The modification itself supplies the recognized feature.

scenes.tts: Once V H L holds H I F 1 alpha, the ligase builds a ubiquitin chain. A red proteasome accepts the marked target and breaks it down. New H I F 1 alpha keeps entering the system. With oxygen, removal keeps its level low.
scenes.caption: Once VHL holds HIF-1α, the ligase builds a ubiquitin chain. A red proteasome accepts the marked target and breaks it down. New HIF-1α keeps entering the system. With oxygen, removal keeps its level low.
scenes.visual: Carry the gripped target forward. Yellow ubiquitin blocks attach one by one into a chain, then the target enters a large red proteasome barrel and becomes small peptide blocks. A level meter beside the conveyor stays low as production and removal continue; label it 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Once VHL holds HIF-1α, the ligase builds a ubiquitin chain. A red proteasome accepts the marked target and breaks it down. New HIF-1α keeps entering the system. With oxygen, removal keeps its level low.

scenes.tts: When oxygen falls, the hydroxylase completes its reaction less often. Fewer H I F 1 alpha molecules gain the badge. V H L finds fewer targets, while synthesis continues. H I F 1 alpha accumulates, pairs with A R N T, and helps switch on low-oxygen genes.
scenes.caption: When oxygen falls, the hydroxylase completes its reaction less often. Fewer HIF-1α molecules gain the badge. VHL finds fewer targets, while synthesis continues. HIF-1α accumulates, pairs with ARNT, and helps switch on low-oxygen genes.
scenes.visual: Thin the gold oxygen dots gradually rather than switching them off. The PHD block badges fewer passing targets, so most green VHL grips remain open. Grey HIF-1α blocks accumulate, then pair with white ARNT blocks at a large gene panel whose indicator rises. Label the response 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: When oxygen falls, the hydroxylase completes its reaction less often. Fewer HIF-1α molecules gain the badge. VHL finds fewer targets, while synthesis continues. HIF-1α accumulates, pairs with ARNT, and helps switch on low-oxygen genes.

scenes.tts: Notice what changed and what stayed shared. Oxygen changed the target feature V H L could read. It did not invent a new ubiquitin or proteasome. Signals change protein fate by changing what an E 3 can recognize.
scenes.caption: Notice what changed and what stayed shared. Oxygen changed the target feature VHL could read. It did not invent a new ubiquitin or proteasome. Signals change protein fate by changing what an E3 can recognize.
scenes.visual: Freeze the reusable yellow ubiquitin stream and red proteasome in their usual positions. Highlight only the gold OH badge and green VHL grip. Collapse the whole pathway into a large three-step diagram: signal changes feature, E3 recognizes target, fate changes.
scenes.narration: Notice what changed and what stayed shared. Oxygen changed the target feature VHL could read. It did not invent a new ubiquitin or proteasome. Signals change protein fate by changing what an E3 can recognize.

scenes.visual: End card on the dark ground with Hex beside one centered line only: 'Signals change protein fate by changing what an E3 can recognize.'
